plot_extraction.response_text:
A miserly old sailor named Thomas Geary falls gravely ill during a voyage from Sydney to London. Determined that no one should inherit his £600 savings, he gives the money to a cabin boy, Jimmy, and orders him to throw it overboard. After Thomas dies, sailors Bill Hicks and the narrator suspect Jimmy secretly kept the money. They search and threaten him until he admits possessing it and claims he hid it inside the second mate’s mattress.

Unable to reach the mattress, Bill secretly buys it from the mate for two pounds, intending to divide the fortune only with the narrator and cheat Jimmy. When the ship reaches London, Jimmy discovers their scheme and insists on receiving his share. Bill and the narrator take the mattress below and cut it open, but find no money. By the time they return to the deck, Jimmy has vanished without collecting his belongings or wages. They realize he deceived them about the hiding place and escaped with Thomas’s fortune.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic maritime yarn told in the first person by an elderly night watchman recalling his years at sea. Its dominant stylistic feature is the narrator’s strongly marked working-class seafaring dialect, represented through dropped initial consonants, phonetic spellings and colloquial grammar: “’ave,” “’im,” “wot,” “arter,” “ag’in,” “six ’undered,” and “we was.” This eye dialect establishes voice, period and social setting immediately. It also makes the tale sound spoken rather than written, as though it were being delivered informally to a listener. Recurrent formulas such as “I says,” “says Bill,” and “then I see” reinforce the rhythm of oral storytelling. The narrator’s grammar is nonstandard, but his account is clear, controlled and shrewd; the contrast prevents the dialect from implying intellectual simplicity.

The narrative voice is genial, candid and morally compromised. The watchman presents greed as a universal weakness while speaking as if he were merely an amused observer, even though he quickly joins Bill’s scheme and demands half the supposed fortune. His opening claim that sailors are seldom miserly prepares an ironic story in which nearly everyone becomes obsessed with money. He habitually softens wrongdoing with comic euphemism and false sentiment. Bill’s attempt to steal the money becomes a “little game,” while threats and searches are framed as concern for “the pore boy.” This gap between what the men say and what they mean is central to the humour. The narrator rarely condemns anyone directly; instead, character is exposed through behaviour, dialogue and self-serving rationalisation.

The prose is plain, economical and event-driven. Descriptive passages are sparse, with only enough nautical detail to make the setting tangible: the barque, fo’c’sle, companion-way, wheel, watches, bunks, dirty weather and East India Docks. Technical language is introduced naturally through the sailors’ experience rather than explained for an outsider. Figurative language is similarly concrete and comic. Getting down the companion-way unseen is compared to removing a man’s false teeth without his noticing, while the unseen hand that supposedly tickles the cook is “the size of a leg o’ mutton.” Such comparisons are domestic, bodily and exaggerated, matching the narrator’s practical imagination.

Dialogue carries most of the characterization and much of the plot. Exchanges are brief, quick and adversarial, with characters constantly bargaining, threatening, teasing or trying to outwit one another. Bill is blustering, greedy and transparently manipulative; Jimmy answers him with literal-minded cheek and increasing confidence; the second mate’s vanity is revealed by how readily he accepts Bill’s absurd flattery. Repetition is used for comic escalation, especially in disputes over whether the money was thrown overboard, where it is hidden, and who can trust whom. Speech often contains a surface politeness that barely conceals hostility. Bill calls Jimmy “my lad” while intimidating him, and Jimmy negotiates shares while insulting Bill’s appearance and intelligence.

The humour is predominantly ironic, situational and character-based. It arises from greed making supposedly experienced adults foolish, while the apparently vulnerable boy remains several moves ahead of them. There is also sustained dramatic irony: Bill and the narrator believe they are manipulating Jimmy, but their increasingly frantic conduct suggests that Jimmy is manipulating them. The story repeatedly converts morally dubious behaviour into farce. A deathbed scene leads not to solemn reflection but to calculations about banknotes; a nocturnal search becomes a misunderstanding about tickling the cook; and Bill’s attempt to obtain the mattress requires an extravagantly sentimental speech about wanting to remember the second mate every night. The understated narration heightens these moments because absurd events are reported with relative seriousness.

Structurally, the tale follows a compact chain of reversals. Thomas’s determination to take his savings with him creates the initial mystery. Jimmy’s claim to have thrown the packet overboard appears to end the matter, but Bill suspects him; Jimmy then admits that he kept it, only to claim that he hid it in the second mate’s mattress. Bill’s ingenious purchase of the mattress seems to promise success, but the final search reveals nothing, and Jimmy disappears. Each apparent solution creates a fresh complication, allowing suspense and comedy to rise together. The repeated searches, threats and failed schemes form a pattern of mounting desperation, while the ship’s approach to London supplies a natural deadline.

Pacing is leisurely at the outset, where the narrator establishes Thomas’s miserliness and illness, then accelerates after the deathbed revelation. From that point, scenes are linked by practical questions—whether Jimmy has the money, where he has hidden it, how the men can reach the mattress and how they can exclude him from the division. Short dialogue exchanges quicken the movement, while summary passages compress the week-long searches and the voyage toward London. The final dockside sequence slows slightly to prolong expectation before delivering the reversal.

Characterization is economical and caricatural without being flat. Thomas is defined by lifelong miserliness, Bill by greedy ingenuity, Jimmy by alertness and nerve, and the second mate by vanity mixed with slyness. Minor figures receive memorable traits in a phrase or two: Walter Jones believes himself medically knowledgeable because his family is always ill, and the cook is “a terrible ticklish man.” These concise tags make the shipboard community vivid and provide material for later jokes. No character possesses clear moral authority. Thomas wastes his life hoarding, Bill and the narrator plot theft, Jimmy is probably a trickster, and the second mate may understand more than he reveals.

The ending is deliberately suggestive rather than explanatory. Jimmy’s disappearance strongly implies that he has escaped with the money, but the second mate’s “kind smile” leaves open the possibility that he discovered it or participated in the deception. The narrator does not resolve the mystery; he closes on Bill trying unsuccessfully to smile back at the mate. This visual image supplies both humiliation and uncertainty. It also preserves the oral-yarn quality, since the pleasure lies less in establishing legal truth than in showing greed punished by bafflement.

Overall, the style combines vernacular narration, compact plotting, nautical realism and dry comic irony. Its moral method is indirect: rather than preach against greed, it lets greed generate suspicion, humiliation and self-defeat. The tone remains amused and unsentimental even around death and attempted theft, producing a characteristic mixture of geniality, cynicism and farce.

generation.response_text:
### The Mattress of the *Mary Ann*

Sailormen, take ’em as a class, ain’t misers. They may spend foolish, and they may spend drunk, and some of ’em will spend the same shilling twice if the landlord ain’t looking; but they don’t often ’oard. A man as goes knocking about the world with all ’is property in a sea-chest soon learns that money was made to move. Leastways, that was always my belief till I sailed in the *Mary Ann* with old Thomas Geary.

I’m night-watchman now, as you know, and my sea-boots ’ave been dry these fifteen years; but I can see Thomas this minute, sitting on ’is bunk and stitching a patch on the elbow of a coat that wasn’t worth the thread. He was a little, bent man, with grey whiskers growing under ’is chin like weed under a pier, and eyes that looked at every mortal thing as if it wanted to borrow sixpence.

We was bound from Sydney to London, a barque of seven ’undred tons, carrying wool, tallow, and one or two passengers that spent the voyage wishing they ’adn’t come. Thomas was an able seaman by rating, though ’e was sixty-five if ’e was a day. He’d been going to sea since ’e was a boy, and according to Bill Hicks he’d never bought so much as a drink for another man.

“Six ’undred pound ’e’s got,” says Bill to me one evening, while we was putting a bit of spun-yarn round the handle of a bucket.

“Who says so?” I says.

“Everybody,” says Bill.

“That means nobody,” I says.

Bill shook ’is head. He was a broad, heavy man, with a mouth made for eating and hands made for taking hold of anything that wasn’t nailed down.

“I know,” he says. “Thomas keeps it in notes, sewed up in a belt round ’is middle. Six ’undered pound. And ’e sleeps with one eye open.”

“He sleeps with both eyes open when you’re near ’im,” I says.

“That’s friendship,” says Bill. “He knows I’m interested in ’im.”

Thomas was close in everything. He’d smoke the last inch of another man’s pipe if ’e could get it, and I’ve known ’im stand ten minutes by the galley waiting for the cook to turn ’is back, so as to warm ’is hands without saying thank you. If a man lost a button, Thomas would look over the side to make sure it ’ad gone before ’e offered sympathy. Yet nobody disliked ’im as much as might be expected. At sea you get used to queer craft, and Thomas was so regular in ’is meanness that it came to be looked on like the ship’s bell or the second mate’s bad language.

About three weeks out he was took ill.

Walter Jones, who fancied ’imself as good as a doctor because ’is wife and seven children was always under one, said it was the liver. The cook said it was the ’eart. Bill Hicks said it was six ’undred pound pressing on ’is stomach.

Whatever it was, Thomas got worse. He went off ’is food, which alarmed nobody, seeing that ’e’d always been careful with other people’s; but when ’e refused a basin of broth that cost ’im nothing, we knew ’e was bad.

The skipper came down once and asked ’im how ’e felt.

“Dying,” says Thomas.

“Cheer up,” says the skipper.

“What for?” says Thomas.

The skipper thought a moment, but not finding an answer, went away.

For two days Thomas lay quiet in ’is bunk. Every now and then he’d put ’is hand inside ’is shirt and feel round ’is waist, and then ’e’d breathe easier. Bill watched ’im doing it, and became so thoughtful that ’e walked into the mainmast.

On the third night the weather came on dirty. The wind was aft, but there was a heavy sea, and the old *Mary Ann* rolled till a man in the fo’c’sle could put on one sea-boot in ’is own bunk and the other in somebody else’s. I had the first watch below and was trying to sleep when Jimmy, the cabin boy, came down the companion-way.

Jimmy was about fifteen, small for ’is age, with a round face and a pair of sharp brown eyes. He looked simple when ’e was standing still, but he didn’t often stand still long enough for anybody to make the mistake.

“Thomas wants me,” he says.

“What for?” says Bill, lifting ’is head.

“Because ’e don’t want you,” says Jimmy.

Bill lay back and said that boys was different when ’e was young. Jimmy passed along to Thomas’s bunk and drew the curtain.

We couldn’t ’ear much owing to the wind and the creaking, but after a bit Thomas’s voice rose sharp.

“Promise!” he says.

“All right,” says Jimmy.

“Swear it!”

“I swear,” says Jimmy.

“Over the side,” says Thomas. “Straight over. Don’t let nobody get it. Nobody! D’you understand?”

“Yes,” says Jimmy.

Then there was whispering, followed by a rustle like paper. Bill sat up again. I didn’t sit up, because I was already sitting, but I leaned forward in a friendly way.

Jimmy came from behind the curtain with one hand inside ’is jacket.

“What’ve you got there?” says Bill.

“Cold,” says Jimmy.

“I ’eard paper,” says Bill.

“Then paper’s wot I’ve got,” says Jimmy.

He started for the ladder, and Bill put out a foot.

“Steady, my lad,” he says. “You might fall.”

Jimmy stepped over it. “Then move your ugly great boot,” he says.

Bill looked at me.

“Boys,” he says, very sad. “No respect for age.”

“You ain’t old enough,” I says.

“No,” says Bill, “but I’m ugly enough, according to ’im.”

Jimmy went on deck. We waited a minute, and then Bill jumped out of ’is bunk and followed. I went too, not from curiosity, but because a growing boy ought not to be alone on deck in dirty weather with anything valuable in ’is pocket.

We came up just as Jimmy was standing by the lee rail. He made a quick movement with ’is arm, and something small and dark went flying from ’is hand into the sea.

“There!” he says.

Bill ran to the rail and stared over.

“What was that?” he says.

“Nothing,” says Jimmy.

“You don’t throw nothing overboard,” says Bill.

“I just did,” says Jimmy.

“Wot was it?”

“Something old Thomas give me.”

Bill’s face changed. “Money?”

Jimmy nodded.

“How much?”

“Six ’undred pound.”

Bill made a sound like a hatch-cover falling on a dog.

“You threw six ’undered pound overboard?”

“Thomas told me to.”

“Why?”

“So nobody could ’ave it.”

Bill gripped the rail. The ship rolled, and for a moment I thought ’e was going after it. I caught ’im by the belt.

“Where did it go?” he says.

“In the sea,” says Jimmy.

“I know it went in the sea. Whereabouts?”

Jimmy pointed astern. “Back there.”

Bill gazed into the darkness as if ’e expected the notes to come swimming after us. Then he turned on Jimmy.

“You wicked young rascal,” he says. “You ought to be ashamed of yourself.”

“I promised,” says Jimmy.

“You shouldn’t make promises like that.”

“Thomas made me.”

“Then you should’ve deceived ’im,” says Bill. “It would’ve been kinder.”

Jimmy gave ’im a long look and went aft to the cabin. Bill stayed at the rail till a sea came over and wetted ’im from the knees down. Then ’e followed me below and sat staring at Thomas’s curtain.

Thomas died at four bells. He went very quiet, with one hand round the old belt, which was empty. Walter Jones listened to ’is chest through a tin pannikin and said there wasn’t much hope. The skipper came down again, looked at Thomas, and said Walter was right.

We buried ’im next afternoon. The skipper read the service, the body slid over the side, and Thomas Geary, who’d spent forty-odd years saving six ’undered pound, went off without a penny on ’im. Bill watched the splash and sighed.

“Pore old Thomas,” he says.

“You’re thinking of the money,” I says.

“I’m thinking of both,” says Bill. “They went the same way.”

For the next two days ’e was very low. He didn’t eat much at breakfast, and at dinner he only ’ad three helpings. Whenever Jimmy passed, Bill watched ’im with a peculiar look.

On the third evening ’e came to me while I was at the wheel.

“He never threw it over,” he says.

“Who never threw wot over?”

“Jimmy. The money.”

“I saw ’im throw something.”

“So did I,” says Bill. “But wot?”

“Something dark.”

“Exactly. Six ’undered pound in Bank of England notes ain’t something dark.”

“It might’ve been wrapped up.”

“It might’ve been a bit of rope yarn,” says Bill. “It might’ve been an old rag. It might’ve been the cook’s sock. All we saw was something.”

“You said you ’eard paper.”

“I did,” says Bill. “Good paper. Valuable paper. And that boy’s got it.”

I told ’im that if ’e believed that, ’e’d better tell the skipper.

Bill was shocked.

“Tell the skipper?” he says. “And get the pore boy into trouble? You’ve got no ’eart.”

“Wot do you mean to do, then?”

“Talk to ’im private,” says Bill. “Give ’im good advice. Save ’im from temptation.”

“And take the money?”

“Only to look after it,” says Bill. “Till ’e’s older.”

I said nothing. Six ’undered pound is a large sum, particularly when you’re earning three pound ten a month and paying for your own tobacco. Bill watched my face.

“Share and share alike,” he says.

“Three shares,” I says. “You, me, and Jimmy.”

“Two,” says Bill. “You and me.”

“It’s Jimmy’s money, if ’e’s got it.”

“That’s why ’e mustn’t ’ave a share,” says Bill. “It would encourage ’im.”

I told ’im I’d think it over, which meant that I already ’ad.

That night we searched Jimmy’s sea-chest. We done it very careful, and put everything back exactly as we found it, except a small apple, which Bill ate to prevent it rolling about. There was no money. We looked under Jimmy’s bunk, inside ’is spare boots, behind the water-breaker, and in an old concertina belonging to Ned Price. The concertina made a noise in the middle of the search, and the cook woke up.

“Who’s that?” he says.

“Nobody,” says Bill.

The cook sat up. “Somebody tickled my foot.”

“Dreaming,” says Bill.

“I wasn’t dreaming,” says the cook. “There’s an ’and under my bunk.”

“That’s your imagination.”

“It’s the size of a leg o’ mutton,” says the cook.

Bill drew ’is hand out and put it behind ’im.

“You’d better go to sleep,” I says. “You’re feverish.”

The cook said he’d show us feverish if ’e was tickled again, and kept awake the rest of the night with a sheath-knife beside ’im. That stopped our searching in the fo’c’sle for a time.

Next day Bill tried kindness.

“Jimmy,” he says, giving the boy half a plug of tobacco, “you know me.”

“Yes,” says Jimmy, looking at the tobacco.

“I’ve always been a father to you.”

“My father washes,” says Jimmy.

Bill swallowed something.

“I’ve took an interest in you,” he says.

“So does the mate when I’m late with ’is boots.”

“What I mean is,” says Bill, “you can trust me.”

“No, I can’t.”

Bill glanced round. “Wot did Thomas give you?”

“Advice.”

“Wot else?”

“Work.”

“Wot else?”

“Six ’undered pound.”

“And wot did you do with it?”

“Threw it overboard.”

Bill smiled at ’im, but there wasn’t any warmth in it.

“Don’t tell lies, my lad.”

“I ain’t.”

“We saw you throw something.”

“That was it.”

“It wasn’t heavy enough.”

“Banknotes ain’t heavy.”

Bill’s smile disappeared.

“Suppose I search you?” he says.

“Suppose I call the mate?”

“Suppose I knock your ’ead off first?”

“You’d get blood on your shirt,” says Jimmy, “and it looks bad enough now.”

Bill raised ’is hand, but I caught it. Not out of mercy, exactly. A boy with ’is head knocked off can’t tell you where ’e’s hid money.

We let Jimmy go, and for a week we watched ’im. Bill watched ’im by day and I watched ’im by night, and between us we got so little sleep that we began suspecting each other. Once I woke and found Bill looking through my clothes.

“Lose something?” I says.

“My knife,” says Bill.

“You’re holding it in your mouth.”

“So I am,” says Bill. “That’s where I put it.”

After that I kept my sea-chest locked, and Bill said it was a strange thing when one honest man couldn’t trust another.

Jimmy went about ’is work cheerful as a cricket. He polished the cabin brass, carried the skipper’s meals, and whistled whenever ’e passed us. That whistle worried Bill more than anything.

“He’s got it,” he says. “No boy whistles like that on twelve shillings a month.”

“Perhaps he’s ’appy.”

“That proves it,” says Bill.

We searched the boats, the chain-locker, and a flour barrel in the galley. The cook caught Bill in the barrel up to ’is shoulders and hit ’im twice with a ladle. We looked behind loose planks and inside coils of rope. Bill even offered to mend Jimmy’s jacket, but Jimmy said ’e’d rather wear the holes.

At last, when we was about five weeks from London, Bill lost patience. He waited till Jimmy came off duty one evening, then caught ’im by the collar and hauled ’im into the sail-locker. I followed to see fair play, by which I mean that Bill shouldn’t frighten the boy into offering less than my proper share.

The lamp swung overhead, making Bill’s face come and go in the shadows. Jimmy leaned against a bundle of canvas and looked bored.

“Now, my lad,” says Bill, “this little game’s gone far enough.”

“What game?”

“You know.”

“No, I don’t.”

“The six ’undered pound.”

“I threw it overboard.”

Bill took hold of ’is ear.

“Say that again,” he says.

“I threw it overboard.”

Bill pulled.

Jimmy kicked ’im on the shin.

Bill let go and danced round the locker in silence, being unable to find words strong enough for the occasion.

“Assault,” says Jimmy.

“Assault?” says Bill, when ’e could speak. “You near broke my leg.”

“You started it.”

Bill shut the door and stood with ’is back to it.

“We know you kept that money,” he says. “We don’t blame you. Any sensible person would. But you’re a boy, and money’s a dangerous thing.”

“It ain’t hurt you,” says Jimmy.

“I never ’ad enough to find out. Now, where is it?”

Jimmy folded ’is arms.

Bill cracked ’is knuckles, one after another. It took some time because ’e had large hands.

“You wouldn’t like us to tell the skipper,” I says gently. “He might say you stole it.”

“Thomas give it to me.”

“To throw away,” says Bill. “If you didn’t throw it away, you disobeyed a dying man. That’s serious.”

“How serious?”

“Six ’undered pound serious,” says Bill.

Jimmy looked from ’im to me.

“If I tell you,” he says, “wot do I get?”

“You get our forgiveness,” says Bill.

“I don’t want it.”

“And a share,” I says.

Bill scowled at me.

“A small share,” he says.

“Three equal shares,” says Jimmy.

“You’re too young for two ’undred pound.”

“I’m old enough for six.”

Bill and me drew apart to talk. Bill said fifty pound was more than enough for a boy. I said the boy could keep quiet for two ’undred or shout for six. Bill said one ’undred. Jimmy called out that ’e could hear every word and the price ’ad just gone up.

In the end we agreed to three equal shares, though Bill did it with tears in ’is eyes.

“Now,” he says, “where is it?”

Jimmy hesitated.

“Safe,” he says.

“Where?”

“In the second mate’s mattress.”

For a moment neither of us spoke.

“The second mate’s mattress?” says Bill.

Jimmy nodded.

“How?”

“The day after Thomas died. The second mate was on deck, and I was cleaning ’is berth. There’s a split at one end. I shoved the packet into the horsehair and stitched it up.”

Bill stared at ’im admiringly.

“That’s clever,” he says.

“I know.”

“It’s also wicked,” says Bill. “Don’t forget that.”

“Get it, then,” I says.

Jimmy laughed.

“You get it.”

That was the difficulty. The second mate, Mr. Small, guarded ’is berth like a dog guards a butcher’s shop. He was a thin, sandy-haired man, very neat in ’is habits, and proud of ’is bedding. Every morning he aired the mattress, every week ’e beat it, and any hand that entered ’is room without leave generally came out quicker than it went in.

“We’ll take it while he’s on watch,” says Bill.

“How’ll we get down the companion-way with a mattress without anybody seeing?” I says. “You might as well take a man’s false teeth out while ’e’s eating.”

“We’ll think of something,” says Bill.

We thought for three days and got nowhere. Then Bill had an idea. Ideas came to Bill slowly, but when one arrived it made ’im restless.

“Buy it,” he says.

“Buy wot?”

“The mattress.”

I looked at ’im.

“You propose going to the second mate and saying, ‘Please, sir, sell me the mattress you’re sleeping on because there’s six ’undered pound inside it’?”

“Not in them words,” says Bill.

“Wot words, then?”

“Leave that to me.”

Next afternoon, when Mr. Small came forward to inspect some work, Bill met ’im looking solemn.

“Beg pardon, sir,” he says, touching ’is cap. “Might I ’ave a word?”

“You’re having several,” says Mr. Small.

“It’s a private matter, sir. Sentimental.”

The second mate looked surprised. Nobody had ever connected Bill with sentiment before.

“Well?”

Bill lowered ’is voice.

“I’ve took a great liking to that mattress of yours, sir.”

Mr. Small stepped back.

“My mattress?”

“Yes, sir. From the first day I saw it.”

“You’ve never seen it.”

“I’ve seen the corners, sir, when Jimmy was airing it. A beautiful mattress.”

Mr. Small looked at me. I turned away and studied the sea.

“Wot d’you want with it?” he asks.

Bill sighed.

“My mother ’ad one just like it,” he says.

“Your mother?”

“Exactly like it. Same shape. Same colour. Same—same stuffing.”

Mr. Small’s mouth twitched.

“She died on it,” says Bill, with a catch in ’is voice. “Last words she ever said was, ‘William, always think kindly of mattresses.’”

The second mate put a hand over ’is mouth.

“And so,” Bill goes on, “I thought if you’d sell me yours, sir, I could sleep on it every night and remember—remember things.”

“Your mother?”

“And you, sir,” says Bill. “Both together.”

Mr. Small turned red and coughed.

“I’m using it,” he says.

“Not after we reach London, sir. You’ll be going ’ome to your family and feather beds, while a lonely sailorman goes to ’is lodging with nothing but memories.”

“You can have it for two pounds,” says Mr. Small.

“Two pound!” says Bill, forgetting ’is mother.

“Take it or leave it.”

Bill’s face worked. Two pound was nearly three weeks’ pay, and paying money to get at money went against all ’is feelings.

“Would fifteen shillings—”

“Two pounds.”

“Suppose one pound five—”

“Good afternoon, Hicks.”

“Done!” says Bill. “Two pounds.”

Mr. Small nodded and went aft, smiling to ’imself.

Bill watched ’im go.

“He’s robbed me,” he says.

“You’ll soon be rich,” I says.

“That don’t make it right.”

We didn’t tell Jimmy about the purchase. It was Bill’s suggestion that we should get the mattress, find the money, and divide it in two before the boy knew anything.

“He agreed to thirds,” I says.

“Under pressure,” says Bill. “A bargain made under pressure ain’t legal.”

“It was you putting on the pressure.”

“That makes it worse,” says Bill. “Besides, ’e insulted my shirt.”

I objected for a while, chiefly because I thought Bill might try to make the two shares into one. At last ’e swore by everything ’e could remember that I should ’ave half. We shook hands, then each counted ’is fingers.

From that day the mattress seemed to grow bigger. Whenever Mr. Small brought it on deck to air, Bill looked at it as if it was a roast goose. Jimmy noticed, of course. There wasn’t much Jimmy didn’t notice.

“Wot are you staring at?” he asks.

“Nothing,” says Bill.

“That ain’t nothing.”

“It’s the second mate’s mattress.”

“I know.”

“I was just thinking it looks comfortable.”

Jimmy gave ’im a sideways glance.

“You ain’t comfortable to look at,” he says, “but I don’t stare.”

As we neared England the wind fell light, and the ship crawled up-Channel with every man talking about ’is pay and what ’e meant to do ashore. Bill and me talked in whispers. We decided to wait till the vessel was secured in the East India Docks. Mr. Small would hand over the mattress, and we’d carry it below, cut it open, and pocket the notes while Jimmy was busy in the cabin.

There was only one question.

“The boy’ll ask for ’is share,” I says.

“Let ’im ask,” says Bill.

“He might go to the police.”

“And tell ’em ’e cheated a dead man, hid six ’undered pound in an officer’s bed, and then lost it? No. He’ll keep quiet.”

Jimmy came up behind us.

“Who’ll keep quiet?” he says.

“The cook,” says Bill.

“Why?”

“He talks in ’is sleep.”

“Wot does he say?”

“Go away,” says Bill.

Jimmy grinned. “You bought that mattress, didn’t you?”

Bill went still.

“Who told you?”

“Nobody.”

“Then you don’t know.”

“I ’eard the second mate telling the skipper. Two pound was cheap, he said, for a mattress and a beautiful memory.”

I had to turn aside.

Jimmy held out ’is hand. “My share.”

“You get it when we get the money,” says Bill.

“Three equal parts.”

“That’s right.”

“And no tricks.”

“Would I trick you?” says Bill.

“Yes,” says Jimmy.

The docks was in sight by then, all masts, smoke, roofs, and grey water. Everybody was busy. Orders came quick; ropes went ashore; men shouted from quay and deck. In the confusion Jimmy disappeared forward, and Bill smiled.

“Good,” he says. “We’ll do it now.”

The moment we was made fast, Mr. Small came down carrying ’is mattress rolled under one arm. He handed it to Bill.

“There you are, Hicks,” he says. “Treat it kindly.”

Bill paid ’im two sovereigns with a look like a man burying twins.

“Thank you, sir.”

“And think of me every night,” says Mr. Small.

“I will, sir,” says Bill. “Depend on it.”

The second mate gave ’im a kind smile. I didn’t like that smile. It was the sort a man gives when ’e knows where the joke is and you don’t.

We carried the mattress below. It was awkward on the ladder and twice as heavy as Bill expected.

“Horsehair,” I says.

“Banknotes,” says Bill, sweating.

We got it into the empty fo’c’sle and barred the door. Bill pulled out ’is knife.

“Which end?” he says.

“Jimmy said there was stitching.”

There was stitching at both ends. We chose one and cut it open. Horsehair came out in a great black lump.

“Careful,” I says. “Don’t cut the notes.”

Bill put in ’is arm up to the shoulder. He felt all round, drew it out, and shook ’is head.

“Other end.”

We cut the other end. More horsehair. Soon the deck looked like a dead pony had exploded. We searched handful by handful. We felt along every seam and tore open the centre. There wasn’t so much as a tram ticket inside.

Bill sat down among the stuffing.

“He’s moved it,” he says.

“Jimmy?”

“Who else?”

“You said ’e couldn’t get at the mattress.”

“Then the second mate found it.”

We looked at each other.

“That smile,” I says.

Bill sprang up. “Find Jimmy!”

We rushed on deck. Men was going ashore, officials was coming aboard, and carts rattled on the quay. We searched the cabin, galley, fo’c’sle, boats and chain-locker. No Jimmy.

His sea-chest stood unopened beneath ’is bunk. His spare clothes was there. His boots was there. Even the twelve shillings wages due to ’im was still in the skipper’s account.

The skipper hadn’t given ’im leave. The mate hadn’t seen ’im go. A dock labourer remembered a small boy slipping across a barge to the quay just after the first line was made fast, but by then London had swallowed ’im.

Bill stood at the gangway, breathing hard.

“He’s gone,” I says.

“With six ’undered pound,” says Bill.

“Maybe.”

“He never put it in the mattress.”

“Maybe not.”

“Then why tell us ’e did?”

I looked at the torn mattress, which we’d dragged halfway up the companion-way in our hurry.

“To keep us busy,” I says.

At that moment Mr. Small came along. He looked at the horsehair sticking from the mattress and then at Bill.

“Not comfortable?” he asks.

Bill opened ’is mouth, but nothing came out.

“You’ve been altering it,” says Mr. Small. “Pity. It was a very good mattress.”

“Did you ever find anything in it, sir?” I asks.

“Find anything?”

“A packet, perhaps.”

Mr. Small’s eyebrows went up.

“No,” he says. “Should I have?”

Bill stared at ’im. The second mate stared back. Then ’e smiled that same kind smile again and walked away.

Whether Jimmy took the money ashore, whether Mr. Small found it first, or whether old Thomas’s six ’undered pound really did go over the side that dirty night, I can’t tell you. Bill always said Jimmy ’ad it, and for years afterward ’e studied every well-dressed young man he saw in London, hoping to recognise the cabin boy.

As for the mattress, Bill kept it. He ’ad to, after paying two pounds. He stitched it up himself, but ’e never got the horsehair even, and for six months ’e slept with a lump under ’is back as big as a pig.

“Reminds you of your mother?” I asks him once.

“No,” says Bill.

“The second mate, then?”

Bill looked at me very bitter.

“Every night,” he says.

And that’s the worst of being greedy. You may get nothing for it, but you generally get something to remember it by.

The Clockmaker of Bellwether Street

Every clock in Mr. Vale’s shop told a different time.

The tall walnut grandfather clock beside the door insisted it was twenty minutes past three. The silver carriage clock in the window claimed midnight. A row of brass alarm clocks shouted contradictory hours in bright red numerals, while the tiny watch pinned beneath a glass dome had not moved from six forty-two in nearly thirty years.

People often asked Mr. Vale why he did not synchronize them.

“They are not soldiers,” he would reply. “There is no reason for them to march together.”

Then he would bend over his workbench and return to whatever delicate task occupied him: fitting a spring, polishing a gear, or listening with a stethoscope to the private heartbeat of a watch.

Bellwether Street was narrow, crooked, and old enough to remember when horses had outnumbered people. Its buildings leaned over the road like neighbors sharing gossip. At one end stood the railway station; at the other, the gray clock tower of Saint Orison’s Church. Between them were a bakery, a tailor, a bookshop, three houses, and Mr. Vale’s clock shop.

The painted sign above his door read:

VALE & DAUGHTER  
CLOCKS REPAIRED  
TIME RESTORED

There had never been a daughter, as far as anyone knew.

The people of the town had invented explanations. Some said Mr. Vale’s daughter had died young. Others said she had quarreled with him and gone abroad. Mrs. Pembrook, who sold bread two doors down, believed the sign had been left by a previous owner and that Mr. Vale was too lazy to repaint it.

Mr. Vale answered no questions about the matter.

He had lived alone above the shop for forty-one years. Every morning at eight, he opened the blue door. At one, he ate soup. At seven, he closed the shutters. On Sundays, he walked to the river and scattered crumbs for ducks, though he never attended church.

His routine changed on a wet Tuesday in October, when a girl named Iris Bell came into the shop carrying a broken clock.

She was twelve years old, small for her age, and dressed in a yellow raincoat. Water ran from her dark hair onto the floorboards. In her arms she held a round kitchen clock with a cracked white face.

Mr. Vale looked up.

“You are dripping on the nineteenth century,” he said.

Iris glanced at the floor. “Sorry.”

He handed her a cloth.

“Dry yourself, then the nineteenth century.”

She obeyed. After wiping her face and hair, she knelt and rubbed the floorboards until they shone.

Mr. Vale extended one thin hand toward the clock. “Let me see.”

Iris placed it on the counter.

The clock was cheap, made of faded green plastic. Its hour hand hung loose, pointing permanently downward.

“It fell,” she said.

“Clocks seldom fall without assistance.”

“I knocked it off the wall.”

“Then you fell it.”

“Can you fix it?”

Mr. Vale turned the clock over. “Almost anything can be fixed.”

“How much?”

He named a price.

Iris stared at him. “I have three pounds and sixteen pence.”

“That presents a difficulty.”

“I could work for the rest.”

“I do not employ children.”

“You have ‘and Daughter’ on your sign.”

“That is not an advertisement for a vacancy.”

“I can sweep. And clean windows. And make tea.”

“Can you repair a balance wheel?”

“No.”

“Cut a replacement pinion?”

“No.”

“Recognize a French striking movement?”

“No.”

“Then your usefulness is uncertain.”

Iris met his eyes. “I learn quickly.”

Something in the shop clicked. Then something else clicked in reply. Rain whispered against the window.

Mr. Vale pushed the clock back toward her.

“Three pounds and sixteen pence,” he said. “And six Saturdays.”

“Doing what?”

“Discovering whether you learn quickly.”

That was how Iris Bell became the first assistant Mr. Vale had ever permitted behind the counter.

She arrived the following Saturday at seven fifty-five, wearing the same yellow coat. He gave her a broom and instructed her to sweep without touching anything.

This was harder than it sounded. The shop was so crowded that even the dust had to squeeze between objects. Clocks covered every wall. They stood on shelves and hung from hooks. They occupied cabinets, windowsills, and chairs. There were solemn clocks, ridiculous clocks, jeweled clocks, plain clocks, and one carved like a cat whose eyes moved from side to side with each tick.

By ten, Iris had broken nothing.

Mr. Vale regarded this as promising.

He taught her how to open the back of a watch without scratching it. He showed her gears no larger than snowflakes and springs as fine as eyelashes. He explained that clocks did not measure time itself.

“Nothing measures time,” he said. “A clock measures its own movement and invites us to call that time.”

Iris frowned. “Isn’t that the same thing?”

“Is a map the same thing as a country?”

“No.”

“Is a recipe the same thing as a cake?”

“No.”

“Then a clock is not the same thing as time.”

Mr. Vale placed a brass gear in her palm.

“Time is what happens,” he said. “A clock is what watches.”

By the end of her first Saturday, Iris had learned to clean a mainspring. By the end of her second, she could identify six kinds of clock by sound alone. The kitchen clock was repaired during the third week, but she continued coming to the shop.

Neither of them mentioned the original agreement.

At home, the clock returned to the wall above the table. Iris’s father barely noticed.

Daniel Bell had once been a loud, laughing man. He had taught music at the secondary school and played the piano at every town festival. But since Iris’s mother had died two years earlier, he had become quiet. He moved through the house like someone searching for a room that was no longer there.

He no longer played the piano.

Sometimes, after dinner, Iris found him sitting in the dark, looking at nothing.

The broken kitchen clock had belonged to her mother. Its ticking had filled every breakfast, every argument, every hurried morning before school. When Iris knocked it from the wall, the sudden silence had terrified her. She had felt, absurdly but completely, that she had broken the last living piece of her mother.

Now it ticked again.

Her father looked up at it one evening.

“You had it repaired.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He lowered his gaze to his untouched tea.

Iris wanted him to say more. She wanted him to smile, to tell her that her mother would be pleased, to stand and play something bright on the piano. Instead, the clock ticked above them, measuring the distance between their chairs.

Winter settled over Bellwether Street.

Iris spent every Saturday with Mr. Vale. He remained strict, but his strictness gradually acquired kindness around the edges. He kept ginger biscuits in a tin and pretended not to notice when she ate three. He found a magnifying lens that fit her eye. When she solved the problem in a Victorian mantel clock—a bent tooth in the escape wheel—he nodded once and said, “Adequate,” which she understood to mean excellent.

In December, while searching a cabinet for oil, Iris found a photograph.

It showed Mr. Vale as a young man, though she recognized him only by his sharp nose. Beside him stood a woman with a wide smile. Between them was a little girl in a white dress, holding a wooden clock shaped like a house.

On the back, written in blue ink, were the words: Elianor, Mara, and Rose. Summer, 1958.

Mr. Vale took the photograph from her hand.

“You were told to look for oil.”

“I’m sorry.”

He placed the picture in a drawer.

“Was Rose your daughter?”

His face became still.

“You may go home early today.”

“But—”

“Now, Iris.”

She left without finishing her work.

The following Saturday, she almost did not return. Shame kept her awake the night before, replaying the moment in the cabinet. But at eight, she stood outside the blue door.

Mr. Vale opened it.

For several seconds, neither spoke.

Then he stepped aside.

“There is a regulator clock in the back room,” he said. “Its pendulum suspension is damaged.”

Iris removed her coat.

They worked in silence until noon. At last, while she held the pendulum rod steady, Mr. Vale spoke.

“Rose was my daughter.”

Iris did not move.

“She died when she was nine,” he continued. “Scarlet fever. Quick as a match burning. Her mother survived her by eleven years, though not in any meaningful sense.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Yes. People often are.”

He adjusted a screw with careful fingers.

“Why is her name not on the sign?” Iris asked softly.

“It is.”

She thought of the words above the door.

“And Daughter.”

“The shop was meant to be hers. She liked mechanisms. At five, she dismantled a pocket watch with a kitchen knife. Ruined it entirely.”

He smiled, but only for an instant.

“After she died, I painted the sign. My wife thought it morbid. Perhaps it was. But grief requires a place to live. If you do not give it a room, it occupies the whole house.”

Iris thought of her father sitting in the dark.

“Does it ever go away?”

“No.”

Her heart sank.

Mr. Vale looked at her.

“But it learns manners,” he said. “Sometimes.”

That winter was the coldest in thirty years. The river froze from bank to bank. Snow softened the roofs, buried the tracks, and turned Bellwether Street into a white corridor.

Then, on the first Thursday of February, the clock in Saint Orison’s tower stopped.

It stopped at six forty-two in the morning.

At that same minute, every clock in Mr. Vale’s shop stopped as well.

Mr. Vale was upstairs making tea when the sound vanished.

For forty-one years, he had lived surrounded by ticking. He no longer heard it consciously, just as a sailor does not hear the sea. But when it ceased, the silence struck him like a blow.

He ran downstairs.

Pendulums hung motionless. Second hands rested between marks. The cat clock’s eyes stared to the left. Even clocks disconnected from the tower, clocks powered by batteries, weights, springs, or electricity, had stopped at six forty-two.

All except one.

Under its glass dome, the tiny watch that had shown six forty-two for thirty years began to tick.

Mr. Vale stared at it.

The watch had belonged to Rose.

It had stopped at the hour of her death.

Now its second hand moved.

He lifted the glass dome with trembling hands.

The bell above the shop door rang. Iris rushed in, breathless.

“The church clock—” she began, then saw the shop. “What happened?”

Mr. Vale did not answer.

Rose’s watch ticked in his palm.

Then the minute hand moved forward.

Six forty-three.

“No,” he whispered.

Iris stepped closer. “Mr. Vale?”

He closed his fingers around the watch.

Outside, people gathered in the street. Doors opened. Faces turned toward the silent church tower. An uneasy murmur spread through the town.

The baker entered the shop without knocking snow from her boots.

“Vale, the tower clock has stopped,” Mrs. Pembrook said. “And so has mine. Every one in the bakery. Tom says the station clocks are frozen too.”

Mr. Vale looked around his motionless shop.

“What time is it?” Mrs. Pembrook asked.

No one replied.

The question traveled through Bellwether Street. People checked telephones, but their screens displayed six forty-two. Computers showed the same. At the railway station, the electronic board froze. Radios played music, but no announcer gave the hour. Trains halted outside town because signal systems had failed.

Only the little watch continued.

At seven twelve by Rose’s watch, Mr. Vale climbed the church tower with Iris behind him.

“You should stay below,” he said.

“You’ll need someone small enough to reach inside the movement.”

“I will not.”

“You usually do.”

He lacked time to argue.

The tower stairs spiraled upward through cold darkness. Dust lay thick on the steps. Above them, the giant clock mechanism waited in a wooden chamber behind the faces of the tower. Its gears were green with age, each one larger than a dinner plate. Iron rods stretched toward the four motionless hands outside.

Mr. Vale inspected the escapement.

“Nothing is broken,” he said.

“Then why did it stop?”

“Because something is broken.”

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“It describes most of life.”

He checked the weights, cables, teeth, and bearings. Everything was in order. Yet the pendulum refused to move. When he pushed it, it swung once and stopped as if caught by an invisible hand.

Rose’s watch ticked in his waistcoat pocket.

Iris heard it.

“Why is that watch still working?”

Mr. Vale’s expression warned her away, but she persisted.

“It was already stopped, wasn’t it? Before today.”

He turned toward the mechanism.

“It belonged to Rose.”

“What time did she die?”

The tower chamber seemed to grow colder.

“Six forty-two.”

Iris looked through the dusty glass at the town below. People stood in clusters in the snow. With no clocks to obey, no trains to catch, and no school bells to answer, they waited helplessly.

“What if the watch isn’t measuring time?” she said.

Mr. Vale glanced at her.

“You told me clocks only measure their own movement. Maybe all the other clocks have stopped because time here has stopped. But this watch is measuring something else.”

“What?”

“I don’t know. Her time?”

“Rose has no time.”

“Your grief, then.”

He stiffened.

Iris almost apologized, but did not.

The watch ticked between them.

Mr. Vale removed it from his pocket. It read seven twenty-nine.

“My grief does not control the clocks of Bellwether.”

“How do you know?”

“Because grief is not magic.”

“Neither are clocks stopping all at once.”

Mr. Vale opened the back of the watch. The balance wheel turned smoothly. Beneath it, engraved inside the case, were words he had never seen.

He held the watch closer to the window.

“What does it say?” Iris asked.

He read aloud.

“When you are ready, let the morning continue.”

The handwriting was his wife’s.

Mr. Vale sat heavily on a crate.

For years after Rose’s death, Elianor had repaired clocks beside him. She had been the better craftsperson, patient where he was stubborn, intuitive where he was exact. This watch had stopped on the morning Rose died, and neither of them had touched it again.

Or so he had believed.

Perhaps Elianor had tried to repair it. Perhaps she had succeeded and then fixed it in place, waiting for a day she knew her husband could not yet imagine.

Iris sat beside him.

“What happened at six forty-two?” she asked.

“My wife called me from upstairs. Rose was ill. The doctor had said the fever might break by morning. I was in the shop, working.”

“On what?”

“A music box. A customer wanted it before noon.”

He stared at the turning gears of the little watch.

“Elianor called my name. I said I would come in a moment. I was fitting a pin. A ridiculous piece of metal. I heard her call again.”

He stopped.

“When I went upstairs, Rose was gone.”

“You couldn’t have known.”

“I knew she was ill.”

“You thought there was time.”

“Yes.”

The words broke something open in him.

“For sixty-three years,” he said, “I have woken at six forty-two. Every morning. No alarm. I hear Elianor calling me. Every morning, I think that if I move quickly enough, I might reach the room before the second call.”

Iris looked at him with tears in her eyes.

“But you can’t.”

“No.”

The watch ticked.

Below, the town waited in a morning that refused to advance.

Iris took his hand.

“My father stopped playing the piano when my mother died,” she said. “He says he doesn’t want to, but I think he’s afraid.”

“Of what?”

“That if he makes music, it means the world is allowed to keep going.”

Mr. Vale closed his eyes.

The watch showed seven thirty-seven.

“How do I let the morning continue?” he asked.

Iris considered this.

“Maybe you don’t fix anything.”

He gave a tired laugh. “That is a poor suggestion to make to a clockmaker.”

“Maybe that’s why you need it.”

She pointed to the open watch.

“Let it run.”

Mr. Vale’s fingers tightened around the case.

For decades, he had preserved the hour of Rose’s death beneath glass. He had told himself it was remembrance, but now he understood that it was refusal. He had built his life around a minute and called the prison a memorial.

To let the watch run felt like losing her again.

Then, faintly, he remembered Rose at five years old, laughing over the pieces of the ruined pocket watch. He remembered her hands black with oil. He remembered summer light, Elianor singing, and the three of them eating cherries above the shop.

None of those memories had happened at six forty-two.

He closed the watch and placed it on the mechanism of the tower clock.

“All right,” he whispered.

At once, the giant pendulum swung.

A gear turned.

Then another.

The mechanism shuddered into motion. The minute hand outside lurched forward, and the bell above them struck once.

Across Bellwether Street, clocks awakened.

In kitchens, stations, classrooms, and shops, second hands jumped forward. Telephones flashed. Radios announced the time. The cat clock’s eyes rolled right. The entire town filled with ringing, chiming, buzzing, and ticking.

Every clock resumed at seven thirty-eight.

Rose’s watch continued with them.

Mr. Vale bowed his head.

Iris stood beside him until the bells stopped.

Spring came early that year.

The story of the frozen clocks became a town legend, though no two people told it the same way. Mrs. Pembrook blamed an electrical storm, despite the absence of lightning. The vicar called it a miracle. The stationmaster insisted it had been foreign interference.

Mr. Vale offered no explanation.

He changed in small ways. He began taking lunch outside when the weather was fine. He allowed customers to bargain. Once, he closed the shop on a Wednesday and went to the coast for no reason anyone could discover.

Rose’s watch remained on his workbench, still ticking.

Iris continued her apprenticeship. By fourteen, she could repair a marine chronometer. By sixteen, she could make parts Mr. Vale’s aging hands could no longer manage. Her father sometimes came to collect her, lingering near the door and examining the clocks.

One evening, he noticed an old music box on a shelf.

“Does it work?” he asked.

Mr. Vale looked at Iris.

“It does now,” she said.

She wound it. A slow melody filled the shop.

Daniel Bell listened without moving. Then he went home, opened the piano, and played for the first time in four years.

The music drifted through the walls while Iris sat on the stairs and cried quietly, not from sorrow alone.

Years passed.

When Iris was twenty-three, Mr. Vale brought her outside before opening time. The painted sign above the blue door had been taken down.

“I thought you were having it cleaned,” she said.

“I was.”

A workman across the street turned the sign around.

It now read:

VALE & DAUGHTER  
CLOCKS REPAIRED  
TIME RESTORED

Beneath the old lettering, in smaller gold letters, someone had added:

I. BELL, CLOCKMAKER

Iris stared at it.

“People will think I’m your daughter.”

“People have thought more foolish things.”

She looked at him. His hair was entirely white now, his shoulders bent, but his eyes were clear.

“Is this your way of saying you want me to stay?”

“No. It is my way of admitting you already have.”

She hugged him.

Mr. Vale endured this with the awkward patience of a man waiting for bad weather to pass. But after a moment, he placed one hand gently on her back.

Above them, Saint Orison’s clock began to strike eight.

Along Bellwether Street, shutters opened. The baker set warm loaves in her window. A train whistled at the station. Somewhere, a piano began its morning scales.

Mr. Vale unlocked the blue door.

Inside, the clocks ticked at different speeds and displayed different hours. Some were fast, some slow, and some awaiting repair. Rose’s watch rested beneath its glass dome, no longer frozen at six forty-two.

It kept imperfect time, gaining almost a minute each day.

Mr. Vale never corrected it.

Not every clock needed to be right.

Some only needed to go on.
